identity.real_world_identity_notes: Customer GT3 racing car based on the F13 M6 with the 4.4 litre twin-turbo V8, campaigned by privateer teams from 2016. Ricardo, which engineered the unit, describes a semi-automatic transverse transaxle carrying a sequential six-speed plus reverse racing gearbox in a magnesium casing, shifted by paddles. BMW's later fully automatic centrifugal clutch was a Zanardi-specific adaptation, not the baseline customer car.

wheel_rim.notes: BMW's official cockpit media does not textually identify a wheel-mounted rev/shift-light array; dashboard or display indicators are not treated as wheel equipment.

notes: A first-person drive of the baseline M6 GT3 explicitly requires the clutch to get moving. BMW separately documents a hydraulic clutch; its later fully automatic centrifugal clutch was a Zanardi-specific adaptation and does not redefine the baseline car.
No throttle lift is required on upshifts and no manual blip on downshifts, because the drive detected automatic cut and automatic blip. This matches every other curated paddle-shift GT3 car.
Observed live in AMS2 1.6.9.91 via guided verification observation ams2.bmw-m6-gt3.20260813t155203395z-7c40ce55 by Jason Kinslow.

overrides.condition: AMS2 1.6.9.91 accepted clutch-free move-off with automatic clutch and shifting disabled.
AMS2 1.6.9.91 models shift lights on the M6 GT3 wheel.

confidence.basis: Direct cockpit inspection during the guided drive.
Simulator behavior was live-tested in AMS2 1.6.9.91 with automatic clutch and shifting disabled, and the real-world six-speed sequential paddle transmission is established by a registered source.

notes: Observed live in ACC 21257365 via guided verification observation acc.bmw-m6-gt3-2017.20260823t012449446z-3dfbf616 by Jason Kinslow.

overrides.condition: ACC accepted the guided full-throttle clutchless upshift while the authentic lift claim remains open.
ACC models no shift lights integrated into the M6 GT3 rim, unlike AMS2.

confidence.basis: Direct cockpit inspection during the ACC contribution drive.
Ricardo establishes the M6 GT3 transmission. ACC reported the exact M6 GT3, its stable internal id and GT3 class; the guided drive directly established ACC behavior and cockpit.

claims.basis: BMW's official cockpit media does not textually identify a wheel-mounted rev/shift-light array. Its customer-racing brochure specifies status LEDs on the wheel and identifies them with control/status functions, not rev/shift indication; dashboard or display indicators cannot settle wheel integration.
The registered source establishes the real-world identity and transmission, and the exact simulator identity was observed live.
The transmission engineer specifies a paddle-shifted semi-automatic sequential six-speed transaxle; the live drive confirmed six paddle gears and clutch-free move-off.
Directly observed during the guided drive: running-shift clutch use, automatic cut and blip, and the cockpit rim.

BMW establishes the baseline car's hydraulic clutch and an exact-car first-person drive explicitly requires clutch use to get moving. BMW's fully automatic centrifugal clutch is documented only for the special Zanardi adaptation.
Telemetry name `BMW M6 GT3 2017`, internal id `bmw_m6_gt3`, and class `GT3` identify the F13 customer racer already curated from Ricardo and AMS2 evidence.
Directly observed during the guided drive: move-off, shift clutch use, automatic cut and blip, and the cockpit rim.

notes: The wheel-rim shape was originally recorded as "gt-style". The separate "gt-style", "formula" and "prototype" values described the same rim: molded grips at 9 and 3 with a control face between them, usually carrying a display and rev lights. They are merged into "gt-formula". The rim was not observed again and nothing about the observation changed.
driver_summary: Six-speed sequential engineered by Ricardo. It cuts the upshift and blips the downshift, but you still need the clutch to pull away, unlike its M4 GT3 successor.
